Three Championships, One Trophy: My Emerald Steel Journey in Disney Lorcana

Frank Karsten qualified for three different continental championships and successfully conquered Brazil! Check out his tournament journey across the world, and why Emerald Steel was the perfect weapon for his triumph!

By Frank Karsten

|@karsten_frank
|

Published Sep 24, 2026

|

19 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

This past month, I've been on an incredible journey across multiple continents and Disney Lorcana Championships. Following a 6-3 finish at the North American Championship and a 6-3 finish at the European Championship, I once again brought my trusty Emerald Steel to the Brazil Championship and came away with the trophy!

In this article, I'll take you through my tournament and travel experiences, show how my decklist evolved from event to event as I anticipated metagame changes, and highlight some of the dazzling collectible promo cards I picked up along the way.

The North American Championship

The North American Championship unfolded at the Disneyland Hotel in Anaheim on August 29–30. Most of the 136 competitors, including myself, qualified by finishing in the Top 32 of a North American Disney Lorcana Challenge earlier in the season. As a result, the level of competition was exceptionally strong.

I prepared for the event with the World Class Cards crew, sharing results and ideas in the weeks leading up to the tournament. After first exploring the metagame and experimenting with various brews in early August, each team member assigned a score to every deck to reflect how likely they were to consider it for the championship. Tallying up those numbers let us quickly narrow the field down to three primary contenders: Amber Emerald Royalty, Emerald Steel Midrange, and Amber Amethyst Ramp.

Once we had come to that conclusion, I did plenty of structured in-person testing with Rob de Haan in the Netherlands, and our results indicated that Emerald Steel Midrange was favored against Amber Emerald Royalty (also known as Princess Aggro). Meanwhile, the matchup against Amber Amethyst Ramp seemed slightly unfavored to even, depending on how many anti-Evasive cards they had. This left us feeling confident that Emerald Steel had a solid overall matchup spread against the decks we expected to face most often.

Potentially tricky, less popular matchups such as Amber Steel Songs, Amber Emerald Circle of Life, Amber Emerald Book Control and Amethyst Ruby Evasive proved no worse than roughly even in our testing, while we were favored against Emerald Amethyst Retro Evolution Device and against Emerald Sapphire Mouse. Taken together, this yielded an encouraging matchup spread, given the expected metagame.

What's more, I thoroughly enjoyed the playstyle. I had previously won DLCs with Strength of a Raging Fire decks that aimed to curve out with characters on the first few turns, sing Strength of a Raging Fire to wrestle control of the board, then challenge or quest ahead to victory. Elinor - Renowned Diplomat rewarded this playstyle just as well, so it was a natural pairing. While I had also tested a few games with an Emerald Steel version featuring the combination of Paradise Falls - Exotic Destination and Touch the Sky as well, these cards weren't early-game characters and therefore did not help Strength or Elinor reach their maximum potential. They were cut from the deck without much fuss.

By the weekend before the North American Championship, Emerald Steel had already emerged as my frontrunner. That same weekend, a high-profile Championship Challenge Qualifier was held at Woodz Shack TCG, where the finals featured an Emerald Amethyst Retro mirror match and the Top 8 included two Amber Emerald Book Control decks. I reckoned that this event would substantially shape the metagame at the North American Championship, and the developments seemed like welcome news.

Given those results, Emerald Steel did not seem to have a target on its head, and after the addition of several item removal characters, it had a good matchup versus those breakout item-based decks. Meanwhile, it had a favorable matchup against the Amber Emerald Royalty deck that I figured players might bring to counter that Top 8 metagame, and I hoped that the deluge of Retro and Book decks would scare many players away from Amber Amethyst Ramp, thereby reducing the metagame share of my worst matchup.

I arrived in Anaheim several days before the tournament weekend, where we had an awesome team house with a spacious table for testing and a sparkling pool for a little Hakuna Matata between games. Thanks to Robert for setting it up and to Mark for the delicious cooking! While the days were filled with playtest games, discussions on the best lines of play in every matchup, and debates on the final card inclusions, I also took the opportunity to visit Disneyland.

Together with teammates Jeff and James, I visited Disney California Adventure Park for half a day. It's always a joy to soak up the atmosphere and ride the attractions. For me, this was a special visit because out of the 12 Disney theme parks in the world, this was the only one I had never visited before. I am grateful that Disney Lorcana gave me the perfect opportunity to do so. Now, after traveling across the world for TCG events over the past 20 years and coincidentally visiting Disney parks along the way—really just a fun theme park day once every two years or so while attending a TCG event in a nearby city—I can now proudly say that I've been to all of them!

Looking back, my favorite parks are Disney's Animal Kingdom and EPCOT, as I especially enjoyed their nature and travel themes. In terms of rides, the best ones I've experienced are Star Wars: Rise of the Resistance and Guardians of the Galaxy: Cosmic Rewind. Yet while the novelty is now gone for me, I still hope that future Disney Lorcana Championships will keep happening at Disney parks because they provide such an ideal environment for the game.

But ultimately, I was there to compete in the Disney Lorcana TCG tournament. So, here is the decklist I registered:

This list had much in common with the Emerald Steel decks that finished in the Top 8, but I made a few notable departures. I felt that ten one-drops was the minimum number required to curve out consistently. Lists with just 4 Tod - All Alone and 4 Darkwing Duck - Crime Fighter would miss a turn-one play too often, which is simply unacceptable in a Strength/Elinor curve-out deck. I settled on 2 Pegasus - Gift for Hercules as a result. 

While its low willpower is a liability against opposing Elinor - Renowned Diplomat, there are certain evasive-heavy opening hands against non-Elinor decks where Pegasus becomes my preferred one-drop, giving the card some useful optionality. Alternative one-drops like Flynn Rider - Spectral Scoundrel and Omnidroid - V.8 lacked that optionality value and always felt weaker to me in testing.

I included three copies of Aladdin - Doing His Part to improve my matchups against decks with Retro Evolution Device or My Adventure Book. It also served as a reasonable backup two-drop on the curve, especially in matchups where Ursula - Deceiver had no targets or where I wanted to guard against an opposing Under the Sea. For these reasons, I preferred it over Benja - Guardian of the Dragon Gem.

To round out my three-drop slot, I used two copies The Huntsman - On the Queen's Orders. Ward was especially relevant against opposing Strength of a Raging Fire or Elinor - Renowned Diplomat, and its lack of Evasive meant that I could try to sidestep The Horseman Strikes!

The presence of that card looms over deck building like the Headless Horseman himself. Some players tried overloading it by adding additional Evasive characters. Other players shaved cards like Mushu - Stealthy Dragon entirely in an attempt to reliably turn an opposing Horseman into a dead card. As for me, I didn't want to commit to a specific plan; I prefer keeping my options open, so I can craft a different plan for every matchup and every opening hand. 

For example, against Emerald Amethyst Retro, I aimed to ink The Huntsman - On the Queen's Orders and play Mushu - Stealthy Dragon; against Amber Amethyst Ramp, I typically aimed to do the opposite. My build for the North American Championship tried to strike a balance while maximizing the most powerful cards available.

While many players ran He Hurled His Thunderbolt or multiple copies of The Terror That Flaps in the Night, I chose three copies of Max Goof - Rebellious Teen. I ran a single copy of He Hurled His Thunderbolt for the longest time and still view it as an efficient answer to Elinor - Renowned Diplomat or Cheshire Cat - Inexplicable, but if you're curving out on the play, it can be tough to fit in an uninkable card that you can't sing before turn five.

Max Goof - Rebellious Teen is inkable and offers a similar effect on turn five, with a free character as a bonus. You do need to find Strength of a Raging Fire reliably, but I tend to mulligan for that card aggressively. If I don't have a solid one-drop or two-drop in my opening hand, I won't hesitate to alter all seven cards and dig deeper for a Strength of a Raging Fire in the process. As a result, Max Goof performed wonderfully for me.

The Terror That Flaps in the Night can be an excellent tool for sniping Grandmother Willow - Ancient Advisor or Hamm - Piggy Bank when you're on the draw. However, its inclusion comes at the expense of characters, which Strength and Elinor need to reach their full potential. I found room for only a single copy at the North American Championship, as I was unwilling to trim any more characters at any slot in the curve.

Finally, I included a lone copy of McHorn - Ice-Cold Officer since I wanted to run five copies of Broadway - Sturdy and Strong in my curve, but the deckbuilding rules only let me play four. Either bodyguard protects my characters, has massive stats in Steel mirrors, and triggers Elinor - Renowned Diplomat more consistently on turn five. While Broadway is generally superior thanks to its willpower and lore pips, McHorn was a capable backup, and in some games against an opposing Broadway or Mrs. Incredible - Super Stretchy, it performed even better.

The deck performed admirably. I finished in 23rd place with a 6-3 record, earning stunning foil promo cards. Besides the foil Stand Out promo for all attendees, I took home a foil Down in New Orleans as my Top 64 prize, and a foil The Headless Horseman - Cursed Rider promo as my Top 32 prize. These cards have gorgeous foiling and true exclusivity as prizes for top finishers at one of the Continental Championships this year, and have become treasured additions to my collection.

The European Championship

I hadn't qualified for the Asia Championship, so the next tournament on my schedule was the European Championship. It took place at the Disney Hotel New York – The Art of Marvel in Paris on September 12–13. Most of the 200 competitors, including myself, qualified by finishing in the Top 32 of a European Disney Lorcana Challenge earlier in the season. Once again, this made for a fiercely level of competition.

While my solid result with Emerald Steel at the North American Championship made it one of my frontrunners for the European Championship, I wasn't automatically locked into the deck. Instead, I kept a close eye on metagame trends. To illustrate this dynamic, let's call Emerald Steel Midrange "rock", an anti-Evasive Amber Amethyst build "paper", and a broad group of decks including Amethyst Emerald Retro, Emerald Sapphire Mouse and Amber Emerald Royalty, "scissors".

Under this framework, here's how the metagame evolved from weekend to weekend:

  • August 29–30: At the North American Championship, the metagame and tournament was dominated by rock, so scissors did poorly. Paper ultimately claimed the title.
  • September 5–6: At the Asia Championship, the metagame and tournament was dominated by last week's paper winner. Rock was poorly positioned as a result, while scissors ultimately clinched the trophy.
  • September 12–13: At the European Championship, I expected the metagame and tournament to be dominated by the previous week's scissors winner. In that case, rock would be a well-positioned choice, and that prediction turned out to be correct.

Of course, this is a simplified model. For example, Amber Emerald Royalty is closer to "anti-scissors scissors" because it's good against Amethyst Emerald Retro and Emerald Sapphire Mouse, yet weak to Emerald Steel Midrange. Still, despite these simplifications, the overall idea and the insights it yields are sound.

The metagame works a bit like the Mad Hatter's tea party, with everyone shifting one seat over to follow last week's winner. Generally speaking, you can expect the deck that beats last weekend's metagame to soar ahead in popularity the following weekend. If last weekend's metagame had a lot of paper, then many players might fear bringing rock to the next event. However, many top competitors will usually try to defeat last weekend's dominant deck by, in this case, bringing scissors. By anticipating that and being one step ahead, rock can become the perfect choice.

Although I tested plenty of Emerald Sapphire Mouse in the week leading up to the event, this logic helped me settle once again on Emerald Steel for the European Championship.

When preparing for competitive tournaments, dedicating time to testing is invaluable, but you also need to give your brain a well-deserved break and ensure you arrive relaxed. So together with teammates Rob and Justin, I visited Disneyland Paris on the Thursday before the championship, which that week happily featured a special Disney Lorcana event.

By completing a Collection Quest, making a Disney Lorcana purchase and joining a Scavenger Hunt, I was able to obtain three French-language promo cards: Buzz l'Éclair – Assurer la Couverture (Buzz Lightyear – Providing Cover), Elsa – Le Cinquième Esprit (Elsa – The Fifth Spirit), and Mickey Mouse – Champion d'Ambre (Mickey Mouse – Amber Champion).

It was a fun experience, and I loved seeing Disney Lorcana being featured so prominently in the parks. I would have preferred English-language promo cards, as awarded at Hong Kong Disneyland Resort, yet these exclusive French promos are still lovely additions to my collection.

But once again, I was there to compete in the Disney Lorcana TCG tournament. So, here is the decklist I registered:

This list closely resembled my version from the North American Championship, but I made several small changes. We had seen the online rise of Emerald/Sapphire Mouse (also known as Mouse House) in the preceding week, so I wanted to be ready for Mickey Mouse & Minnie Mouse - Adventuring Duo. I found the matchup to be favorable, especially if you let them quest once or twice before giving them three free ink, but Rapunzel - Tower Defender was a valuable answer, and I added two copies.

To make room, I shaved one copy of The Queen - Devious Disguise and one copy of McHorn - Ice-Cold Officer, thereby keeping my curve roughly unchanged.

I also anticipated a notable rise in the popularity of Chernabog - Unnatural Force, since it's one of the cleanest answers to Mickey Mouse & Minnie Mouse - Adventuring Duo. When facing Chernabog, it can be extremely valuable to put a character into your discard early, so I added the fourth copy of Launchpad - Trusty Sidekick (cutting my singleton The Terror That Flaps in the Night) alongside two copies of Bobby Zimuruski - Spray Cheese Kid (cutting Pegasus - Gift for Hercules).

I also made some minor tweaks, shaving an Aladdin - Doing His Part and a White Rabbit - Late Again to add another copy each of Ursula - Deceiver and Angela - Night Warrior. Both of those cards performed well for me in North America.

With my list now relatively low on Evasives, my plan at the time against Amber Amethyst was to avoid playing any Evasives at all if possible, neutralizing their The Horseman Strikes!

The deck once again performed beautifully. Though I lost two win-and-ins for Top 16 in Rounds 8 and 9, I still finished in 26th place with a 6-3 record, and I even had the pleasure of meetting Donald Duck along the way!

In the Netherlands, the weekly Donald Duck magazine is a beloved cultural phenomenon that has achieved almost legendary status among Dutch readers of all generations. Most comics focus on Donald, Scrooge McDuck, Huey, Dewey, and Louie, or Gyro Gearloose, and the stories are often packed with modern jokes and allusions to Dutch current affairs. So, I especially appreciated Donald showing up at the Disney Lorcana championship.

The Brazil Championship

Finally, the Brazil Championship took place in São Paulo on September 19–20. Most of the 34 competitors, including myself, qualified by finishing in the Top 16 of one of the two Brazilian Disney Lorcana Challenges earlier in the season. Since many seasoned overseas competitors had traveled to those Challenges, the level of competition was extremely strong, with roughly a quarter of the players at the Brazil Championship already holding a World Championship invite.

Predicting the metagame wasn't easy. While I knew many of the competitors and their deck choices across recent weeks and months, that didn't mean that they would stick with the same decks. They could easily try to go in a different direction or next-level everyone. In fact, when the dust settled, many competitors switched away from decks that they had played in recent tournaments. 

My best guess for the metagame was that it would be around a quarter Amber Amethyst, another quarter Emerald Steel, another quarter Princess Aggro and Mouse House, and a final quarter other decks such as Steelsong, Retro, Circle, and so. This guess turned out to be reasonably close to the truth.

In that field, I figured that Emerald Steel was still respectably positioned. Moreover, I could draw on my extensive experience with the deck. And as always, as an Ultimate Guard sponsored player, I trusted a sturdy Sidewinder deck box to carry my cards and a set of Katana sleeves to protect them.

Here's what I brought: 

The main difference compared to my list from the European Championship was that I added a heftier Evasive package, going up to four copies of Pegasus - Gift for Hercules and four copies of White Rabbit - Late Again. At the European Championship, Thiago Santana and Fabrice Bailleux found great success with a version featuring full playsets of these cards and a plan of going fully Evasive against Amber Amethyst, at least on the draw.

Until then, my plan had typically been to avoid playing Evasives against The Horseman Strikes! However, when trying to set up battles on the ground, I often found myself struggling against their high-willpower characters and damage movement effects. Overloading their Evasive hate was a viable alternative strategy—they might take down one or two Evasives favorably, but then the others could still quest to victory. I tested it the day before the Brazil Championship together with Alphos, and we went 8-8 against DKP's Amber Amethyst deck, which was good enough to convince me to sleeve it up.

To support the plan, you need enough card draw to find plenty of Evasive characters, so I brought back the third copy of The Queen - Devious Disguise. Alphos went as far as adding several copies of You Broke My Smoulder, cutting Broadway - Sturdy and Strong in the process. I opted not to do that because I never wanted to draw multiple copies of You Broke My Smoulder and because I still admired the high willpower and board impact of Broadway - Sturdy and Strong, especially against Steel decks. Still, the overarching idea was similar.

To make room for these additional Evasive early drops, I trimmed Bobby Zimuruski - Spray Cheese Kid and Rapunzel - Tower Defender, in part because I expected fewer Mouse House decks than the previous week. I also cut the fourth Angel - Experiment 624, the fourth Launchpad - Trusty Sidekick, and the second Aladdin - Doing His Part to free up more space. I considered shaving more copies of Launchpad - Trusty Sidekick since an uninkable non-Evasive early drop is a dreadful draw when you're trying to spam Evasives against Amber Amethyst, but I ultimately decided to keep him (supported by two copies of Darkwing Duck - Shadowy Superhero) because I liked the card in various other matchups, and I think that choice worked out well enough during the tournament.

With the benefit of hindsight, the only thing I would have done differently was to retain the fourth copy of Angel - Experiment 624. There was more Amber Emerald Royalty than I had expected, and Angel - Experiment 624 is one of the best ways to punish their Mike Wazowski - Heroic Climber. I probably should have cut one copy of The Queen - Devious Disguise instead. If you're interested in picking up Emerald Steel, then that would be the list I'd recommend for next weekend's events.

After six rounds of Swiss and a Top 8 playoff, I emerged victorious!

Though it was a relatively small event, the weekend reinforced how the game remains wonderfully deep strategically, with decisions every turn on inking, combat, sequencing, and so on. I still notice myself making small errors every match, and I know I still have room to improve my technical play.

Still, I was able to reach the Top 8, and then I defeated Bruno's Amber Amethyst 3-0 in the quarterfinals with the Evasive plan, defeated Federico's Aggro deck 3-0 in the semifinals, and finally beat Clément's Circle deck 3-1 in the finals. I was on a roll, and it was as if a Fairy Godmother slipped the cards right into my hand when I needed them. Yet especially with my girlfriend Alice cheering for me on site, Brazil holds a special place in my heart, and I'm proud to have earned the trophy there.

The Outlook for the World Championship

I am now a three-time premier event champion, having won DLC Lille in 2024, DLC Milwaukee in 2025, and the Brazil Championship in 2026. I'm not the only player to have earned at least three such titles in three regions, as Zan Syed, Ed Chiu, and Dillon LeDuc have also accomplished this feat. Now, we'll have the chance to add another chapter to that legacy at the World Championship.

When the World Championship takes place from December 4–6 in Hawaii, we will enter the tournament with plenty of accolades, but the field is stacked, and the competition will be fierce. One way or another, it'll be a fitting conclusion to a thrilling second season of Disney Lorcana's premier play, and the third season promises to be just as exciting. For me, it will be another memorable chapter in a journey that has already taken me farther than I ever could have imagined.

item.title: The 10 Cards Everybody Wants from Usurp The Shadow Throne
item.description:

The 10 Cards Everybody Wants from Usurp The Shadow Throne

Did you say 1 in 120,000 packs?!?

By Scott Mines

|@HowlingMines
|

Published Sep 25, 2026

|

8 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Flesh and Blood's latest set is in stores now! The landmark twentieth booster covers the penultimate chapter of the War of the Monarch storyline: the biggest overarching narrative since the game began over seven years ago. Imagine Avengers: Infinity War if it was stuffed with shadows, body horror and raising the dead. It's a bit like that. 

Truthfully, this set has been eating up real estate in my brain for months. I've become hyper fixated on the alluring Viserai, the Forsaken, but it's clear that everybody from Ser Boltyn, Breaker of Dawn to Levia, Shadowborn Abomination has emerged from the darkness with a wealth of new support. It's pretty darn incredible. 

That's to say nothing of the collectability of this product. Sure, there's plenty of folks who began building collections around this story arc back in Monarch, but Flesh and Blood has been constantly evolving since that point — and it's clearly evolving again. We know FaB 3.0 is just around the corner and the gradual shift away from fabled cards and into highly exclusive marvels is just beginning, but you can see some of the effects of that transition woven into the fabric of Usurp the Shadow Throne. 

As players and collectors alike are readying up to get their hands on Flesh and Blood's smash hit set, it's as good a time as any to highlight which cards sit as the hottest hits from Usurp the Shadow Throne. Some of these are personal grails and the highlight of any collection, while others look to have an immediate impact on the competitive metagame. Which will be more coveted when the dust settles? We'll have to wait and see. 

Until then, these are the 10 cards you should be hoping to find in your booster packs of Usurp the Shadow Throne. 

Honorable Mention: Usurp the Shadow Throne (Marvel) 

Look, I'm going to be straight with y'all: there's too many sick cards in this set. 

I could have written a list of about thirty different cards that I'd be ecstatic to open from Usurp the Shadow Throne, but after culling down the list it felt a little disingenuous to not include the card with the name of the set — especially when it has a ridiculous marvel variant.

The moment of Viserai's ascension (and Chane's untimely demise) is captured perfectly by Esty Swandana, and it doesn't hurt that the card is a beating against specific opponents. 

The only reason it didn't crack the top ten is because I'm unsure where the price is going to settle. We don't have a great precedent for marvel legendaries that you're allowed to register three of! 

#10: Arknight Shard 

Usurp the Shadow Throne somehow set two new records for fabled cards. It contains two of them, and it's also the end of them. 

Arknight Shard hasn't seen a printing since Crucible of War, but with Viserai returning as the big bad, a reprint was sorely needed. Hopefully this non-foil variant can help bring the price down on what looks to be a must-have tool for Viserai, the Forsaken. 

Personally, the original still looks cooler, but I'm overjoyed to see Isuardi Therianto on a gem. Truly one of the most prestigious names in our game today. 

#9: Blessing of Suraya

I've been saying it for years: Ser Boltyn, Breaker of Dawn was eventually going to... well, break. When a hero has access to tools like Lumina Ascension and Beacon of Victory, it doesn't take much to finally turn the dial to dangerous. 

LSS have avoided it for years, but I think the selection of cards offered to Boltyn this set might finally be the breaking point. 

Blessing of Suraya allows Boltyn to turbo-charge in one single turn via his equipment and other offerings in the "Blessing" cycle like Blessing of Aegis. In multiples, this can create upward of eight Ponder tokens. 

If you can line this up, you can just take a turn off and "pass" to draw eight or more extra cards, playing one gigantic, disgusting hand with an untold damage ceiling. When paired with the power spike from Banneret of Swordsmanship and Bravery of the Blade, I think Boltyn is likely one of the better decks in the format. 

#8: Circlet of Eternal End

If you prepare for what's coming, you'll rarely be disappointed. 

Circlet of Eternal End is a clear, generic safety valve for the rule-breaking shadow nonsense that Usurp the Shadow Throne is about to unleash. When the darkness finally arrives to conquer the Classic Constructed metagame, you're going to want to have a copy loaded in your binder ready to go. 

It also just so happens to make heroes like Katsu, the Wanderer weep tears of genuine pain — so there's that too! 

#7: Soul of Existence (Rainbow Foil)

Both fabled cards are so low on the list? Why?!

Well, a few reasons. Firstly, it's my list. I like to make sure it's a balance of big money collectibles and must-haves that have potential to skyrocket in price. Second, I'm actually not all that impressed by Soul of Existence from a gameplay perspective. 

To be clear, it's the sickest thing in-universe. The only pitch-four card in the game? The cause of Viserai vs Chane. It's so cool. I'm just not seeing that power realized by our new Shadow heroes so far. That said, it looks to be at its best in Levia, Shadowborn Abomination. 

There's also a third reason... but you'll have to wait until Number 1 for that. 

#6: Blasmophet, the Insatiable Hunger (Marvel) 

I will never successfully pronounce Blasmophet correctly. Trust me, I've tried.

That won't stop the premium version of Levia's new best friend from commanding an insatiable price tag though. The Shadow Brute is finally stealing the meta spotlight, part in thanks to this sweet new token. 

Blasmophet allows you an unrelenting resource engine if you keep it fed and is positioned to be a pivotal part of what makes Levia (and future versions of Levia) tick at the competitive level. 

As the game shifts focus onto marvel cards as the pinnacle of collectability, I would snap one of these up now if you're the type of person who loves to flex the bling at the tournament table. 

#5: Become the Shadow Lord (Marvel) 

Just look at it, guys. Holy. 

Become the Shadow Lord's unquestionably a staple card for Viserai, the Forsaken as gate generation, runechant generation and ferrying cards into the banish zone are all boxes that the hero is looking to tick. That's great for the regular version, but the artwork on the marvel variant just absolutely slaps. 

What are you looking at? Just take my money and go. Only come back if you find this artwork on a playmat. A++ to Athiwut B. 

#4: Fallen Herald

Fallen Herald gets my vote for "card that will age like a fine wine" right up until people start smashing my head in with the bottle. 

When it comes to lore nerds like me, the implications of this card are bleak. When it comes to my dreams of chipping my opponent down with runechant tokens, they might be even more bleak. Fallen Herald is a defence reaction in a trenchcoat that can happily be split across damage sources and spit back out with a Gate to I'Arathael token. It's an absolute monster. 

Oh. Be sure to keep an eye on Dimenxxional Ferrymen with this one, too. How'd you like the sound of never taking damage ever again, hmm? 

#3: Violent Gusto

Command and Conquer. The Weakest Link. Heck, even Erase Face if you squint. Violent Gusto is joining the club of 6-power generic attacks with a backbreaking on-hit effect in specific metagames — and it's a club that tends to be worth a ton of money. 

When this one bottoms out, I am jumping on the train for as many copies as I can get. You're guaranteed to blow away whatever aura might be causing you a problem, but threatening to demolish the entire stack of runechants or Gate to I'Aratheal tokens is downright rude. 

Violent Gusto is the kinda card where you're never upset to own a set. Simple as. 

#2: Viserai, the Forsaken // Viserai, Usurper (Marvel) 

It didn't need to go this hard. It has zero business going this hard. 

Adult Hero Marvels are always amongst the most coveted cards in Flesh and Blood, but Viserai, the Forsaken // Viserai, Usurper is setting a new bar when it comes to demand. Not only does the hero rock, but the card is absolutely jaw dropping. 

It's also the only adult marvel in the set on account of Levia, Shadowborn Abomination appearing in the World Championship Souvenir Package and Malice, Domina of the Dead leading the charge in Gem Pack 6. If you open one, scream with joy. If you're not keeping it, I'm right here. 

#1: Soul of Existence (Marvel) 

But this? This is something else. You ain't never gonna see a market price on this thing. 

It's been heralded as "The Gem to End All Gems" by James White himself. Soul of Existence is something special: a uniquely labelled, in-universe language rendition of the cause of the War of the Monarch. It's the only fabled card to ever receive a marvel variant — the perfect transition point between the end of the rarity and a new-found focus on marvel cards. 

It is, without question, the single rarest Flesh and Blood card ever printed. The marvel variant of Soul of Existence is confirmed to appear only once in every 120,000 packs. That's once in every 5,000 boxes. This card is going to remain the ultimate grail amongst Flesh and Blood collectors for a long time, maybe forever. It's a thing of beauty. 

If you're wondering? I have a standing offer of $12,000 for a copy. There are public offers sitting at $10,000 USD. This card is going to be rewriting the history books for years and you'd better have your eyes on it.

How to Build Skull Archfiend of Chaos in Yu-Gi-Oh's Genesys Format

Try some crazy lines and bridge the gap between Fiends and Sacred Beasts with Hanko's Genesys latest brew.

By Hanko Chow

|

Published Sep 30, 2026

|

11 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Recently, I was fortunate enough to participate in the Latin American Remote YCS. While I do usually tend to avoid this kind of event since I believe it was meant to be for Latin American participants, I just wanted to find the most competitive and accessible event to try my new deck at. I would like to thank the tournament organizers and judges for their patience with me and allowing me to play even though I don't speak their native language. Even though I won all three of the last rounds of Swiss in day two, I unfortunately only finished ninth due to tiebreakers. Nonetheless, I'm still pretty happy with my performance with this deck and I'm excited to showcase it!

How to Build Skull Archfiend of Chaos in Genesys

The idea of the deck started out with the realization of how broken Skull Archfiend of Chaos really is as a package. This monster, when it goes to the graveyard, activates to send the Ritual Spell for cost to add another Ritual Monster. Sending Light and Darkness Ritual allows you to add Magician of Dark Chaos - Black Chaos, which can later help you reuse a Spell, or Black Luster Soldier - Soldier of Light and Darkness, which can be a hassle for some decks to deal with. Somehow, Skull Archfiend of Chaos is unpointed in Genesys while there's only five points on Light and Darkness Ritual. Getting Skull Archfiend of Chaos into the graveyard is easy depending on the deck. If it's in your hand or you have a copy of Fiendish Rhino Warrior, any way to discard them to the graveyard will trigger it. This is doable with Fusion Summoning or the next most popular engine right now in Genesys, the Sacred Beast retrains from Chaos Origins.

Calamity of the Sacred Beasts - Hamon, Lord of Striking Thunder, Infinity of the Sacred Beasts - Raviel, Lord of Phantasms and especially Sacred Beasts Released are all very low pointed cards, with only two each on the Hamon and Raviel retrains and surprisingly no points on the Spell that searches for three cards! By using these cards alongside Summoner of the Sacred Beasts (five points), you can easily summon two Sacred Beasts and sometimes draw two cards off Fallen Paradise of the Sacred Beasts before Xyz Summoning Varudras, the Final Bringer of the End Times (20 points) for the destructive omni-negate. This concept of combining Sacred Beasts and Skull Archfiend of Chaos is slowly trending to top tables since it gives you an immense amount of card advantage in your hand while also summoning huge threats! For only five points, any deck can summon these Ritual Monsters that are unaffected by card effects unless they target them.

Unfortunately, you won't always have access to Skull Archfiend of Chaos in the Sacred Beast build unless you also commit points to playing Mercurium the Living Quicksilver (10 points). This also means you'll want to play the other Sacred Beast support cards like Martyr of the Sacred Beasts and Sacred Beasts Thunderclap, which both cost three points per card. By attaching the Skull Archfiend of Chaos to Mercruium, and then sending it for the Field Spell effect, you almost get the same value as when you start with both. I wasn't a big fan of this version since it seems too costly to play. I wanted a deck that can afford to play all the best and affordable hand traps in the Genesys metagame. Mulcharmy Fuwalos (eight points each) is a must-have even though it's not good against Blitzclique, while Skull Meister, D.D. Crow (two points each) and Ghost Ogre & Snow Rabbit (four points each) are all great in most matchups.

With that in mind, I still wanted to focus on taking advantage of Skull Archfiend of Chaos and the Light and Darkness Ritual package. This led me to the next best synergy in the format - Chimera Fusion. This concept has already been showing success since YCS Montreal with the likes of Kyle Waterman and Ram Sighn's builds. Mirror Swordknight is one of the strongest Normal Summons in the game, so I built my own version of it to try it out.

After building these decks separately, I came to the realization that I could just put these two concepts together. By taking out the costly Martyr of the Sacred Beasts Normal Summon and the bricky Sacred Beasts Thunderclap, I built a pile which I personally believe to feature the lowest amount of point costs for the highest reward value. After testing the 60-card build for a while, I found a way to bridge Chimera Fusion cards into Sacred Beasts so long as I open up the Skull Archfiend of Chaos or Fiendish Rhino Warrior with my Mirror Swordknight or Gazelle the King of Mythical Claws. Unfortunately there isn't a real bridge from Sacred Beasts into Chimera Fusion, but you'll often just draw into the Chimera cards from Fallen Paradise of the Sacred Beasts or win without them. Here's the list I brought to the Latin American Remote YCS!

Skull Archfiend of Chaos Decklist

Here's a brief summary of the game plan: the Normal Summon is Mirror Swordknight or Gazelle the King of Mythical Claws, which are very powerful when you combine them with Skull Archfiend of Chaos or any Fiend since you can eventually use Berfomet the Mythical King of Phantom Beasts to send the Skull Archfiend of Chaos or any other valuable piece to connect the engines. If you open with Sacred Beast cards, you can make Varudras, the Final Bringer of the End Times without your Normal Summon while also drawing two cards off Fallen Paradise of the Sacred Beasts.

Both engines are high value and if you open both engines, you can make an incredibly near-invincible end board that can potentially even out play popular board breakers like The Winged Dragon of Ra - Sphere Mode or Lava Golem since there are a lot of layered interactions.

I say it's nearly invincible because the end board also features the Diabell duo package since Gazelle can search for Diabellze the White Witch, which is very easy to summon and filters you through Curse of Diabell and Filia Diabell to get the necessary banishes for Diabellstar Vengeance. Having both Vengeance and White Witch on field will grant your monsters protection from destruction effects while Magician of Dark Chaos - Black Chaos protects your Spell and Traps, making your end board indestructible so that Blitzclique can't touch you.

Not only that, but we're backing it up with Varudras, the Final Bringer of the End Times for the omni-negate and even D/D/D Wave High King Caesar (20 points) to negate two Special Summon activations since it's the best value for two Level 6 Fiends. The backrow will usually have Chimera Fusion and maybe even Sacred Beasts Combined Assault in case you need Inferno of the Sacred Beasts - Uria, Lord of Searing Flames's Spell Trap removal or Hamon to protect your life points.

Starting the game off with Chimera the King of Phantom Beasts not only takes away a random card from your opponent's hand but having that reborn effect during your opponent's turn will either cost them a Skull Meister or can reborn something useful. Usually they'll want to break the destruction protection from the Diabell duo so reborning one of them with the Chimera can be useful. Alternatively, if there's a scenario where multiple monsters get cleared, you can technically summon Infinity of the Sacred Beasts - Raviel, Lord of Phantasms with the Chimera so that Sacred Beasts Combined Assault can also be an omni-negate.

Chimera Fusion is also very useful as another method of disruption depending on the scenario. The most common Fusion I summon has to be the new Nightmare-Eyes Restrict as it takes any combination between Spellcaster, Fiend or Illusion to summon and will equip a monster without targeting. Since Magician of Dark Chaos - Black Chaos is a Spellcaster, this Fusion is easy to make, especially if the opponent is throwing a Lava Golem, Santa Claws or their own Radian, the Multidimensional Kaiju onto my field, all of which are Fiends. Predaplant Dragostapelia or even Azamina Sol Erysichthon may also be necessary depending on the situation.

After I make this end board and rip a random card out of my opponent's hand, I usually win the game since there's almost no card combination that can beat all of my unique interactions. I have nearly a 100 percent win rate whenever I draw a combination of Chimera cards and Sacred Beasts. It's possible to draw less optimally at times which luckily only happened a few times throughout this event for me, but even the half boards you make can surprisingly win.

Another reason why I wanted to play this combination of engines is because of how the metagame of Genesys was in the Side Deck. Many players will have targeted hate towards the Sacred Beast cards like The Eye of Truth or Mutually Affured Destruction, so having the Chimera and Ritual of Light and Darkness cards as a secondary method to play helps compliment the deck. It worked out in my favor at times since it also messed up the opponent's Side Deck plan. Now they either side in more cards than they wanted to or draw the wrong ones depending on which part of my deck I open up to play with.

The Bridge Between Chimera and Sacred Beasts

As previously mentioned, there's a way to bridge or search yourself a Sacred Beast card from only having Chimera Fusion cards and the resources from Skull Archfiend of Chaos. Ideally you'll open a combination of either Mirror Swordknight or Gazelle the King of Mythical Claws with either Skull Archfiend of Chaos or Fiendish Rhino Warrior.

In a slightly convoluted method, you'll aim to send a copy of Infinity of the Sacred Beasts - Raviel, Lord of Phantasms alongside Buio the Dawn's Light, which searches for Mutiny in the Sky. You'll gain access to this double send by using Gazelle the King of Mythical Claws's effect to search for any Illusion monster to search for Fleeting Phantom Mask Master instead of the Diabellze. This makes your end board less powerful than if you already had access to the Sacred Beast cards to begin with, but I would feel that a potential omni-negate or two is more valuable than the Diabell duo at times.

By having both Mutiny in the Sky in our hands and the copy of Raviel in the graveyard, you simply need to use Mutiny in the Sky to Fusion summon for The Duke of Demise, then use the Mutiny in the Sky's graveyard effect to send the Duke of Demise to add it back. Now you can use the Duke's graveyard effect to banish itself to recover Raviel! Raviel will search for Hamon, which gets you to Sacred Beasts Released, and you'll be able to access Summoner of the Sacred Beasts and Inferno of the Sacred Beasts - Uria, Lord of Searing Flames to eventually Xyz Summon a Varudras, the Final Bringer of the End Times.

As an aside, while I was studying these possible lines and seeing what I can do with the power of sending any Fiend to the graveyard, I rediscovered the Sky Scourge Norleras and Phantom of Chaos combo, but since we can't just use any two monsters to make Muckraker From the Underworld in Genesys, I had to find another way to get the Phantom of Chaos onto the field. This required the use of Constellar Ptolemy M7 and the extra Normal Summon you get from The Duke of Demise! Maybe someday I could use this combo in Genesys if they don't increase the points on the Chimera Fusion cards.

Deck Building Should Be Fun in Genesys!

I honestly can't wait for the next points update for Genesys. I really hope they increase the frequency of these points update after every YCS since I find the format being solved less appealing to me than when it's unsolved. I did notice their latest blog post addressed how they're going to reevaluate the initial points list from last year, which I'm excited for! Hopefully they reduce the points enough and let me play Floowandereeze as another deck that represents the Tribute Summon mechanic. Having only Monarchs and Clown Crew represent it feels a bit too restricted, especially since Monarchs have received a ton of nerfs over this year.

I also think that Ghost Mourner & Moonlit Chill can go down to four points since I do think it has potential in the format if it was just one point cheaper. Making it cost the same as Ghost Ogre & Snow Rabbit could be interesting. Another random wish I have is if they can find a way to reduce the points on several other banned cards, like Soul Charge being at 50 is just a bit too much. Maybe it can be 35 to 40 points to make it more viable. Even Pot of Greed isn't seeing too much play anymore at 30 points, but I don't know if that's a good comparison.

Those are my thoughts before the new banlist drops. Hopefully you enjoyed this Fiend pile! I did manage to record a deck profile of it so be sure to check that out if you want a bit more insight on what I played. For now, I'll be looking into what Beyond the Brave gives us to make Genesys more interesting!

item.title: Buyer's Guide to Magic: The Gathering Reality Fracture
item.description:
Magic: The Gathering|collecting|finance

Buyer's Guide to Magic: The Gathering Reality Fracture

Which courses to take at Hexhaven, and which ones to avoid altogether.

By Emma Partlow

|

Published Oct 2, 2026

|

8 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

After the back-to-back Universes Beyond sets, Reality Fracture is finally here and on the shelves! The set takes us back to school, but it's a bit dystopian compared to the warmness of Secrets of Strixhaven earlier this year. There's a lot going on with Reality Fracture, and knowing what to buy and where to start can be challenging if you're new to Magic. 

Buyer's Guide to Magic: The Gathering Reality Fracture

Reality Fracture is the latest in-Magic release, and one that concludes an incredible story arc featuring The Theorist, Jace Beleren, Tam, and a bunch of planeswalkers as they traverse through the Echoverse, a harsh mirror of the Multiverse. Reality Fracture is a love letter to everything Magic, as the set brings a unique twist on iconic cards for newer players to appreciate. If you're looking to buy products, the MSRP for Reality Fracture as published by Wizards of the Coast is the following:

  • Play Booster: $5.49
  • Collector Booster: $26.99
  • Multiverse Reforged Commander Deck: $49.99
  • Magic Foundations Commander Deck: $29.99
  • Bundle: $57.99
  • Secret Lair Bundle: $89.99
  • Draft Night: $89.99

Compared to The Hobbit and Marvel Super Heroes, the MSRP is much lower as there's no additional licensing fees baked into the product's price. Reality Fracture is considered to be a typical set size, and has plenty going for it which includes the Magic Foundations Commander Decks to support new player onboarding. All in all, there's something for everyone with this release regardless of player background.

Should You Buy Magic: The Gathering Reality Fracture Sealed Products?

Ultimately, how you choose to engage with a Magic set is up to you and also extends to the budget you have available. As a general rule of thumb, I recommend spending within your means and try to avoid buying Play or Collector Boosters if you're hoping to make profit. That said, Reality Fracture is a powerful set and offers plenty of color bends on iconic cards, which means it's a great set if you're only looking to buy singles.

Reality Fracture is also the last in-Magic set of the year, meaning entrenched players will resonate more with this compared to Star Trek releasing next month. Nauctis: The Sunken Realm isn't out until early next year, meaning there's a reasonable distance between in-Magic releases which can help manage your budget. In my opinion, Reality Fracture is the best Magic set of the year — and I suspect many of the cards will see play in Commander and competitive Constructed in years to come. There's enough depth and creativity going on that it'll be well-received by the community, meaning it's definitely worth picking up some products if your budget allows it.

Reality Fracture Play Booster Box

  • Current Market Price (as of 02/10/2026): $149.07 ÷ 30 = $4.96 per Play Booster

Play Booster Boxes are your usual product that supports every Magic release. Play Booster Boxes contain 30 Play Boosters, and often work out cheaper than buying 30 loose ones. Each Reality Fracture Play Booster contains the following:

  • 5-6 Common cards
  • 1 Uncommon card
  • 1 Common or uncommon card
  • 3 Echoed pairs cards
  • 1 Rare or mythic rare
  • 1 Traditional foil card (any rarity)
  • 1 Non-foil or traditional foil land card
  • 1 Non-foil helper card or double-sided token*

*Note that Wizards have removed Art Cards from Play Boosters, where these now only appear in Collector Boosters. This began with the release of Edge of Eternities last year.

Play Booster Boxes are ideal if you're someone who's wanting to open a ton of cards from the set, or to perhaps host your own Limited event with friends. Play Booster Boxes have also become a fantastic way to play Commander Sealed if you're wanting to keep the casual vibes. As the name suggests, Play Boosters are geared towards gameplay and you won't open as many high-end treatments compared to Collector Boosters. There's a couple of different showcase and borderless cards you can open in Play Boosters, but these won't be as common.

Reality Fracture Collector Booster Box

  • Current Market Price (as of 02/10/2026): $470.46 ÷ 12 = $39.05 per Collector Booster

Collector Boosters are in Reality Fracture, and remain the premium product supporting every Magic release. Each Collector Booster Box contains 12 Collector Boosters and Reality Fracture incorporates the following spread:

  • 4 Traditional foil common cards
  • 2 Foil uncommon cards
  • 3 Traditional foil uncommon echoed pairs cards
  • 1 Traditional foil tower basic land
  • 1 Traditional foil rare or mythic rare card
  • 1 Non-foil rare of mythic rare card (can be a card from Commander: Reality Fracture)
  • 2 Non-foil Booster Fun* cards 
  • 1 Foil Booster Fun card
  • 1 Art card or traditional foil double-sided token

*Booster Fun is an umbrella term used by Wizards to highlight special treatments you can open in some Play Boosters and every Collector Booster. Booster Fun cards often vary with each Magic release, ranging from Showcase, Borderless, Extended Art, and set-specific foil treatments.

Collector Boosters are only worth purchasing if you're keen to own some of the set's most exotic treatments and want to open some fancy cards. As always, I strongly recommend purchasing within your means even though Reality Fracture Collector Boosters are much more affordable compared to their recent Universes Beyond counterparts. What makes the Collector Booster so pricey is these contain many of the chase cards from the set, with a serialized full-art Bloodline Recollector being the card everybody wants to open from Reality Fracture Collector Boosters.

There's some pseudo-serialization going on in Reality Fracture that's also worth mentioning, as many of the mirror break facet foil cards are limited in quantity, with only 6000 copies of the rares and 3000 of the mythic rares in existence. This is something I think a lot of players are missing with Reality Fracture, and could have an impact on secondary market values on release day and beyond. Either way, Collector Booster Boxes are a reasonable purchase if you have cash to burn along with the mindset that you may not make your money back on the pulls. 

Reality Fracture Bundle

If you aren't interested in a Play or Collector Booster Box but still want to scratch the booster-opening itch, then a Bundle can be a good alternative. Each Reality Fracture Bundle comes with the following:

  • 9 Reality Fracture Play Boosters
  • 1 Traditional foil promo card
  • 30 Basic lands
    • 15 Traditional foil basic lands
    • 15 Non-foil basic lands
  • 2 Reference cards
  • 1 Oversized spindown life counter
  • 1 Card-storage box

This is something I say often when covering these Buyer's Guides but remains true with Reality Fracture, Bundles remain some of the more financially safer ways to interact with a Magic release if you're wanting to be sensible with money. They aren't too expensive, but also provide a decent starting point if you're new to the game. You get a pile of basic lands, a spindown die and even a card storage box to store your cards. As a result, Bundles make for a decent gift-giving option as the packaging is appropriate along without being too expensive.

Reality Fracture Draft Night Box

Becoming a mainstay is the Draft Night Box, which introduces a way to play Limited in your own home with friends. Each Draft Night Box contains the following:

  • 12 Reality Fracture Play Boosters
  • 1 Reality Fracture Collector Booster
  • 90 Non-foil basic lands
  • 10 Non-foil double-sided tokens
  • 1 Draft insert

The Draft Night Box centers on Pick-Two Draft which debuted with the release of Marvel's Spider-Man last year, and needs four players instead of the eight you often see in Traditional Draft. The idea is that four players will play Two-Pick Draft and play three rounds, with the winner taking the Collector Booster as the prize. While this product is geared for Limited play, the Draft Night Box offers a really nice starting point if you're looking to play more tabletop Magic in the future, as you get a ton of basic lands and enough tokens to start your journey into the game.

However, the Draft Night Box encourages you to play a different format if you're wanting a break from Commander, as Pick-Two Draft requires four players which is the same as a Commander pod. It's a nice way to break up the routine and allows you to dip your toes into Limited if you're new to Magic. 

Reality Fracture Prerelease Packs

If you're being careful with spending but want to crack open a Play Booster or two, then a Prerelease Pack is a nice alternative. With Reality Fracture, each Prerelease Pack contains the following spread:

  • 6 Reality Fracture Play Boosters
  • 1 Traditional foil rare or mythic rare card
  • 1 Deck box
  • 1 Spindown die

Unlike Secrets of Strixhaven which saw five unique seeded Prerelease Packs, Reality Fracture only has the one despite boasting five colleges for Limited play. This product is for Prerelease events which happen at local games stores a week before a set's global release. However, a store may have excess post-event where they are available to purchase.

Prerelease Packs aren't really meant for gift-giving as they're intended for events, but you might find one for a good price if the set has been out long enough. Alternatively, buying a handful of Prerelease Packs means you can run your own Prerelease-style event if you're unable to attend the event and bring the experience into your own home.

Multiverse Reforged Reality Fracture Commander Deck

  • Read More: Multiverse Reforged Commander Deck Upgrade Guide

Reality Fracture sees one preconstructed Commander Deck this time around, Multiverse Reforged is a four-color option that offers a unique game plan that isn't unfortunately aimed for newer players. Polymorph-like strategies aren't super common in Magic these days, but does mean you're falling into a more controlling playstyle with this deck. Each Multiverse Reforged Commander Deck contains:

  • 1 Ready-to-play 100-card Commander deck
  • 1 Traditional foil borderless face commander Jace, Multiverse Architect card
  • 1 Traditional foil alternative commander Nissa, Leyline Tamer card
  • 98 Non-foil cards (including 16 new-to-Magic cards)
  • 10 Non-foil double-sided tokens
  • 1 Reference card
  • 1 Deck box

One attractive aspect about the Multiverse Reforged Commander Deck is the array of new and exciting cards due to the Reality Fracture's strong themes. For example, The Ur-Sphinx and Niv-Mizzet, Ghost Counsel are some of the highly-anticipated cards for Commander play, and are already seeing strong secondary market movement as a result. While I don't think this deck is great out-of-the-box, it's still a decent purchase if you're looking to break the deck up for singles. 

To expand on an earlier point, I wouldn't recommend this deck if you're new to Magic and looking to purchase a preconstructed Commander Deck. The playstyle this deck brings is a little unconventional, and is not something that presents a solid platform for new player onboarding.

Magic Foundations Commander Decks

  • Buy Now: Magic Foundations Commander Deck: Calling All Angels
  • Buy Now: Magic Foundations Commander Deck: Keen Engineering
  • Buy Now: Magic Foundations Commander Deck: Wretched Ranks
  • Buy Now: Magic Foundations Commander Deck: Tramplesaurus Rex
  • Buy Now: Magic Foundations Commander Deck: Reign of Dragons
  • Buy Now: Magic Foundations Commander Decks (Set of Five)

Releasing alongside Reality Fracture are the Magic Foundations Commander Decks, and these are geared towards supporting player onboarding. Commander continues to be the most popular format to play in all of Magic, so it makes a ton of sense to have a selection of preconstructed decks that you can play straight out-of-the-box. There's five different decks available to collect, one representing each color in Magic. Each Magic Foundations Commander Deck contains the following:

  • 1 Ready-to-play 100-card Commander deck
  • 1 Traditional foil face commander with new borderless art
  • 99 Non-foil cards
  • 10 Non-foil double-sided tokens
  • 1 Reference card
  • 1 Deck box

I'm quite bullish on the Magic Foundations Commander Decks, as these are some of the best introductory Commander products Wizards have produced in quite some time. One thing I really like them is how they include some notable reprints such as Birds of Paradise and Undead Warchief, which in itself brings an approachable way to start a Magic collection.

To that end, these are ideal as a gift-giving option even if the Magic player in your life already knows and plays Commander. These play fantastically well out-of-the-box, and they're intentionally designed to be a single color as it creates an easier experience for new players. After all, a streamlined mana base is the best one.

Reality Fracture Secret Lair Bundle (Releasing October 23, 2026)

Releasing October 23 is the Secret Lair Bundle that is a new product line supporting Reality Fracture's release. It's worth treating this similarly to a Gift Bundle, but does introduce the collectibility of the Secret Lair Drop Series to stores globally. Each Secret Lair Bundle contains the following spread:

  • 6 Reality Fracture Play Boosters
  • 2 Reality Fracture Collector Boosters
  • 2 Traditional foil Secret Lair Bundle promo cards
  • 20 Traditional foil tower basic lands
  • 1 Oversized spindown life counter
  • 1 Card-storage box

One thing that makes the Secret Lair Bundle an interesting addition for Reality Fracture's release is you can open two of ten promo cards, each coming with stylized art you can't find anywhere else. These appear on ten of the chase mythic rares in Reality Fracture, and are:

  • Emrakul, the Exigent Doom
  • Enlightened Confidant
  • Return of the Light Realms
  • Seasoned Cryomancer
  • The Theorist, Jace Beleren
  • Darklight Phoenix
  • Overwrite the Multiverse
  • Craterclaw Colossus
  • Stingcaster Mage
  • Omnipresence

If you're someone who appreciates the Secret Lair aesthetic then this Bundle is for you, but does come at a higher MSRP as it includes a couple of Collector Boosters. It's unclear on the secondary market value of the promo cards in particular, but expect a few of these to be popular additions for Commander (such as Return of the Light Realms).

Top 10 Best-Selling Presales From Magic: The Gathering Reality Fracture

The votes are in, and the Pyromancer is on fire.

By Emma Partlow

|

Published Oct 2, 2026

|

8 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: Bestselling Cards of the Week

It's been almost six months since we've had an in-universe Magic: The Gathering release, but Reality Fracture has everything to become one of the most memorable yet. There's colorful twists and turns on popular characters, such as Fblthp who finally found the way out of Ravnica to Karn nurturing a Mirrodin without the Phyrexians ever existing. Reality Fracture really does ask the question "What If?", bringing with it a plethora of exciting cards geared towards competitive and casual play. 

Top 10 Best-Selling Presales From Magic: The Gathering Reality Fracture

There's been a bunch of sales activity leading up to Reality Fracture's release, but there's always a few cards on the bubble that are worth keeping in mind when making those orders. Samut, Hazoret's Champion is one such card, and comes with an elegant bit of text to grant all creatures you control haste. This isn't anything fancy for sure, but it will be a popular addition in Commander as this is the best on-rate haste enabler printed thus far. 

A similar sentiment applies to Avacyn, Angel of Horror, which happens to be the best-selling card from the Commander: Reality Fracture subset. Avacyn is a much-loved character from Magic's deep history, with her Echoverse version introducing a potent way to recur nontoken creatures you control back to the battlefield upon dying. It's rather on-theme, and will serve well in any black-based Commander decks moving forward. Cruel Calculations may be close to bulk pricing already, but it's another card seeing interest as it has a high ceiling in Mill-based Commander strategies. Apparently rewarding yourself with card draw when you're milling three players seems to be a good rate. With the trends out of the way, let's look at the best-selling cards from Reality Fracture leading up to today's highly-anticipated release. 

#10 Samut, Tyrant of Naktamun

If there's one card that has seen widespread discussion and discourse leading up to Reality Fracture's release, it's Samut, Tyrant of Naktamun. 

Split second is a keyword ability we don't see often and for a very good reason: it means players can't cast spells or activate abilities once a spell with split second hits the stack. This has potential implications for competitive Commander (cEDH), as the format is highly interactive and the utilizing the stack is foundational for gameplay reasons. That said, Samut is extremely soft to an Orcish Bowmasters trigger or two.

It's unclear whether this version of Samut will have the negative impact on Commander as discussed extensively online, but presales dictate that players are keen to find out for themselves. Giving instants and sorceries split second reads inherently powerful, but time will tell if the card lives up to the discussion.

#9 Draconic Visitor

Draconic Visitor is a color bend on Divine Visitation, a popular Commander card that turns any token you create into an evasive threat. As the name suggests, Draconic Visitor converts any artifact token you create into a 5/5 Dragon instead, which has exciting applications alongside Smaug the Magnificent and Smaug the Impenetrable from The Hobbit. Dragons also happen to be one most-played creature type in casual Commander, so having an engine that turns those Food, Clue, and Treasure tokens into threats is one worth having access to in the ninety-nine.

#8 Vigorbloom Charm

The Charms make a return in Reality Fracture, and Vigorbloom Charm is perhaps the best of the bunch. One trait about any of the Charm (or even the Command) cards is that the playability often extends to casual formats as much as it does competitive ones. That said, each of the modes on Vigorbloom Charm are excellent and bring a level of utility that will thrive at the casual Commander tables — especially if you're looking to build Kwia Vigorbloom anytime soon. 

#7 Multiply by Zero

A reference to Divide by Zero from Strixhaven: School of Mages, Multiply by Zero may be one of the most elegant pieces of removal we've seen for a while. Sure, it doesn't remove any creature with a +1/+1 counter, but it's a strong answer to any creature with indestructible. You aren't actually destroying the creature with a card effect. Instead, it essentially dies due to state-based actions. It's a genuinely clever twist on a removal spell, and I'm expecting to see this one crop up in Standard Constructed and could see wider impact once rotation hits with the release of Nauctis: The Sunken Realm early next year. 

#6 Liliana the Faultless

Prim, proper, and frankly irksome throughout the Reality Fracture story is Liliana the Faultless who comes with an interesting mix of abilities referencing Soul's Attendant and Giver of Runes. With the introduction of Kwia Vigorbloom and the hype around her for Commander play, any form of lifegain is a must-have to play alongside the Sphinx, which makes the Echoverse's take on Liliana a popular purchase leading up to Reality Fracture's release. Admittedly, this one is primed to see competitive play as Orzohov Lifegain has been making waves on Magic Online and MTG Arena as of late, as this seems a decent replacement for Aunt May. 

#5 Ghalta the Immovable

Since the release of Lorwyn Eclipsed earlier this year, "Toughness-matters" has become an exciting way to approach Commander due to the printing of Doran, Besieged by Time. It also probably began with Tarkir: Dragonstorm and Felothar the Steadfast, bringing a novel way to deal tons of toughness-based damage at the casual tables. Reality Fracture sees the Echoverse's take on Ghalta in Ghalta the Immovable, who cares about toughness rather than power. 

While this version of Ghalta won't be heading up a Commander strategy anytime soon, it's fantastic in the ninety-nine as it permits your creatures to attack as if they didn't have defender and to assign combat damage based on toughness rather than its power. You do need to have creatures with higher toughness on-average, but Ghalta is a nice way to enable the strategy while also casting the card ahead of schedule.

#4 Flickering Hound

Displacer Kitten this is not, but Flickering Hound is seeing a ton of attention as it can create a ton of value through making the most of those enter the battlefield abilities. This one can only trigger upon casting a creature spell, but it's potent enough that it can do either the value play or the seriously busted play. It's unlikely the Dog will see play in competitive Constructed formats, but this is a must-have for any Commander strategy that utilizes white and a bunch of creatures. 

#3 Ghalta the Unstoppable

We've already had the immovable object, so it makes sense to mention that the unstoppable force in Ghalta the Unstoppable is seeing healthy sales from Reality Fracture. Since her first printing in Rivals of Ixalan, Ghalta has remained a memorable card to play as it plays into the casual space of "play a massive creature and then win" that remains so popular in Magic even today. While this version of Ghalta isn't as potent as Ghalta, Primal Hunger, this one cares about playing creatures with high power and giving those creatures with trample. 

#2 Way of the Pyromancer

Reality Fracture introduces us to Empower Jace: a mechanic that creates a Jace planeswalker token and features two loyalty abilities. Being able to surveil or draw a card on your turn is excellent, and plays out fantastically well in Limited. Another layer to the mechanic is the cycle of cards that add abilities to planeswalkers you control, such as Way of the Pyromancer.

Essentially, Way of the Pyromancer gets you to a Jace token as early as turn two and enables a plus loyalty ability to add one red mana to your mana pool. This is incredible for any planeswalker-centric strategy in Commander, but it also has some mileage in Constructed formats such as Standard, as it could mean you have a Jace planeswalker with three loyalty that can draw you an extra card on the next turn. That's a ton of value packed into two mana, and it's one that's seen extensive interest since revealed earlier this month.

#1 Geist of Saint Thalia

Despite the excitement around Empower Jace, none has been able to beat the Echoverse's take on Thalia in Geist of Saint Thalia. For an uncommon, this reads simple yet powerful — as she comes with the ability to discount any noncreature spell you cast. And yes, this does include artifacts.

This is perhaps one of the more-pushed cost reducers we've seen in a while, and the applications for Thalia are almost endless. This card is bound to see play in Y'shtola, Night's Blessed in Commander, and in any other strategy that has a high density of noncreature spells for that matter. For me, I'm quite excited to experiment with this in Pauper Commander, especially since Giant's Boulder can be cast for zero with Thalia in play. This is the kind of card that I expect to be a valuable uncommon once there's distance with Reality Fracture, as reducing the cost of noncreature spells is an inherently powerful passive ability to have in Magic.

Reality Fracture is out now, where you can potentially open any of these cards in Play and Collector Boosters, Bundles, Prerelease Packs, Draft Night Boxes, and more. There's also a four-color Commander Deck to support the release, along with five Foundations Commander Decks to encourage beginner play and your entry into Magic.

The Biggest Price Spikes in Pokémon This Week - 10/02/2026

Lugia, Jirachi, and other 30th Celebration cards are taking off.

By Corbin Hosler

|@Chosler
|

Published Oct 2, 2026

|

5 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: Movers and Shakers

The first RGB Mews have sold.

$3,500 to $4,000. That's the price range for the sold listings of an RBG Mew, the ultra, one-in-several-thousand-boxes chase rare of 30th Celebration. Although even calling it a chase rare kind of undersells it, because this is such a grail of a pull that most people don't even include the possibility of one when they're opening packs.

But they're out there, and now several of them have sold. The first several copies sold at $3,500 last weekend, and since then a few more have moved closer to $4,000, which is where current live listings are coming in as well. Listings on eBay are also selling in that range, so I think we've officially got a starting point for the most chase Mew ever printed out of a pack.

And what packs they are.

With the generous hit rates, opening the 30th Celebration packs is the best pack opening experience we've seen in quite some time. I actually used this opportunity to give my five-year-old his first Pokémon packs (a Knockout Collection), and he immediately opened a Night Pikachu in it—only for me to follow it up with Special Illustration Rare Mew ex. Incredible memory for us.

As a result of the great word of mouth around the set, plus the massive demand it already had, we're seeing the price on product like Elite Trainer Boxes stay high (around $160) even as most of the singles drop in price.

But not everything in the release is dropping in price. In fact, several cards are bucking the trend and actually climbing in price despite more and more copies coming onto the market every day.

A bit of a surprise when it became the most sought-after card in the set, Classic Collection Lugia has continued its dominance after two weeks of the set's release. This Lugia came out of the gates at an already-pricey over-$200, and most of us assumed that like everything else it would drop in price as more 30th Collection products hit the market. But while that may still happen eventually, it certainly hasn't happened so far. In fact, the Classic Collection Lugia is moving up in price.

This week alone, Lugia went from $300 up to its current Market Price of $325, putting it comfortably ahead of everything else in 30th Celebration besides the mythical RBG Mew. The next most-expensive card is now Charizard at around $200, and then SIR Mew ex at around $150. Charizard itself is also up, having dipped down to $175 briefly after release. Meanwhile, modern chase Magikarp went as low as $105 before popping back up to its current $120 price.

Special Illustration Rare Jirachi ex has been in the news recently, due to its connection with a child named Avery battling cancer. The last video showed Jirachi being pulled, and since then the card has drawn attention as people across the world—including Jirachi artist Akira Egawa—connect with the story.

The price on Jirachi has settled in the $75 range, slightly down from where it was last week. Meanwhile, a few of the top-end cards in the set have begun to fall in price as expected.

Both the Classic Collection Gengar as well as the Special Illustration Rare printing of Gengar in 30th Celebration have fallen over the last week. Maybe the demand for Gengar is being eaten up by the once-$1,000+ Mega Gengar ex from Ascended Heroes, or maybe 30th Celebration simply has so many other good pulls that are commanding the attention right now.

Either way, it's made Gengar more affordable. The Classic Collection Gengar Prime is down to $80 (from $100 a week), while Gengar ex is dipping down below $100 for the first time, a big drop from the $130 it was selling for a week ago. Speaking of the Ascended Heroes Gengar, by the way, it's down a few more dollars this week to a Market Price of $865, a reflection of the increased supply that reprints this year have brought.

On to the hit I'll always remember opening with my youngest! Both Special Illustration Rare printings of Pikachu ex have also fallen off slightly, with Day Pikachu settling down to about $75 and Night Pikachu at $90.

The last card to call out from 30th Celebration as climbing is Greninja. But no, not the Special Illustration Rare Greninja 148, which would make sense, but instead the Greninja BREAK from the Classic Celebration. The SIR Greninja has dropped from $40 down to almost $30, but the BREAK has actually climbed from $10 to $15. Likewise, M Gardevoir-EX has ticked up from $12 to $18 (and while we're at it, the Ruby & Sapphire printing of Gardevoir is up from $60 to almost $100.

But what about the Futuristic Rares? These were in many ways meant to be the chase cards of the set, a rarity alongside Special Illustration Rares at the top and a new pair of cards guaranteed to go up. And maybe most of that will come to pass—but for now, Future Mewtwo is down all the way to around $60 in price, a huge drop from $80 in the last week and miles away from the $120+ it was around release weekend. Future Mew has fared better, but still it's come down from the $120+ it was last week to a respectable $90 today.

Finally this week, let's look at something that isn't Pokémon: 30th Celebration.

If you were playing in a Pokémon tournament in 2004 or 2005, you had a decent shot to come across some packs of POP Series 1. But for the 99% of us who weren't there, your only real chance to come across a Rayquaza—which more than tripled in price this week to $240—from that era is to stumble across it in the secondary market. Same story for Tyranitar ex Holo, which is up this week to a Market Price of over $300, a huge leap from the $180 it was at the beginning of the summer.

See you next week!
